# South Coast Rail Project NEPA Analysis 

## Summary 

The Massachusetts Department of Transportation (MassDOT) South Coast Rail Project aims to restore 52 miles of commuter rail service between Boston and the Massachusetts South Coast in order to enhance public transit systems. Figure 1 shows the project area with existing stations, new stations, new layovers, and reconstructed stations marked along the corridor. In the 2013 Final Environmental Impact Statement (FEIS) for the project, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) and MassDOT analyzed the project for climate change impacts related to sea level rise. The FEIS also included climate change as part of the cumulative impacts analysis in terms of potential climate change effects on biodiversity and threatened and endangered species. The analyses found no significant climate change impacts on the project or in the cumulative impacts analysis. 

## Project Overview 

Southeastern Massachusetts has been the fastest growing region in the Commonwealth, but poor transportation access to the Boston employment market has constrained economic growth in the towns of Fall River and New Bedford. MassDOT has proposed the South Coast Rail Project to enhance public transit connections between New Bedford/Fall River and Boston and between South Coast cities. The South Coast Rail Project is intended to generate new economic

Climate Change in NEPA Case Study 

2

development while preserving environmental resources. Economic development would result from improved access from New Bedford and Fall River to labor markets in Boston and reverse commute access from areas such as Taunton to New Bedford and Fall River. 

The project proposes the restoration of 52 miles of commuter rail service between Boston and the Massachusetts South Coast. Figure 2 shows a bridge over the Taunton River that is part of the existing commuter rail. The FEIS included analysis of three alternatives: the No-Build (Enhanced Bus) Alternative, the Stoughton Alternative (electric and diesel variants), and the Whittenton Alternative (electric and diesel variants). 

## Considering Climate Change within the NEPA Process 

Project Scope 

The FEIS climate change analysis included an evaluation of sea level rise impacts on all project elements, including stations and layover facilities. Separately, the FEIS evaluated climate change impacts on biodiversity and threatened and endangered species as part of the cumulative impacts analysis. 

Approach 

Climate Change Impacts on Project 

In accordance with requirements from the Massachusetts Secretary of Energy and Environmental Affairs, the FEIS considers a sea level rise-related margin of safety for proposed stations partially located within the coastal zone. MassDOT and USACE assessed project elements to determine if they would be subject to inundation from future sea level rise. The expected useful life of the project elements ranges from 25 years for locomotives to 80 years for structures. Future impacts have been evaluated to 2035, the horizon year of the project. The analysis relied on sea level rise projections from the Massachusetts Climate Change Adaptation Report prepared by the Commonwealth’s Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs. That report considered the potential changes in sea level based on several 

“generally accepted climate models and their predictions representing a range of model inputs. ” The projections, used in the FEIS, are for 0.6 to 1.6 feet of sea level rise by 2050 and 1.9 to 6.6 feet by 2100. 

Cumulative Impacts Analysis 

The cumulative impacts analysis assessed cumulative impacts of the proposed project on biodiversity in 2035 from land conversion, habitat degradation, and climate change. The analyses considered reasonably foreseeable indirect effects, including induced growth that would result from the build alternatives. The analysis compared two scenarios of growth in the region: (1) growth under business-as-usual conditions, and (2) growth directed into Priority Development areas based on municipality planning efforts. 

The analysis included climate change in both of these scenarios, and drew from studies that suggest climate change could affect the distribution of plant species, animal habitats, and ecosystem types. Salt marshes, cold-water fisheries, and vernal pools are the most vulnerable elements of the South Coast area. The projected impacts of climate change were included alongside other trends and current or Climate Change in NEPA Case Study 

3

future actions affecting biodiversity, including land conversion and additional habitat degradation, in the 

comparison of the project alternatives’ impacts on biodiversity. The cumulative impacts analysis similarly incorporated climate change into assessment of threatened and endangered species. For example, climate change could contribute to declines in Eastern box turtle and vernal pool species populations. 

Findings 

Climate Change Impacts on Project 

The sea level rise assessment findings are in the FEIS Coastal Zone section. The assessment found no expected direct impacts of climate change on the project. The majority of the non-tidal river and stream crossings are not adjacent to the shoreline and are not expected to be subject to inundation due to a sea level rise of up to approximately 1.6 feet by 2050. The Weaver’s Cove East Layover Facility would be 

located approximately 20 feet above the current shoreline and is not expected to experience inundation even under the highest predicted sea level rise of 6.6 feet by 2100. 

Cumulative Impacts Analysis 

The cumulative biodiversity impacts in 2035 from climate change and other factors would result in little land conversion and habitat loss and create some areas of degraded habitat under both growth scenarios. The FIES also found the cumulative impacts to threatened and endangered species to be a net benefit, as the South Coast Rail Project would include mitigation of effects to species.

17.title: Transportation Supports Economic Development, Opportunity
17.description: The initiation of South Coast rail service last week highlighted the symbiotic relationship between transportation and economic development.
17.content:
_Frederick W. Clark, Jr., right, President of AIM member Bridgewater State University, celebrates the inaugural run of the South Coast Rail with BSU Student Trustee E. Rose and Student Government President Sophia Pinarreta._

**By Brooke Thomson

 President & CEO**

The initiation of South Coast rail service last week highlighted the symbiotic relationship between transportation and economic development.

The new service will provide connections for people in Fall River and New Bedford who work in Boston; for people in Boston who take jobs on the South Shore; and for people in both locations who may find employment at companies in between. Not to mention new options for students at AIM member Bridgewater State College.

Transportation and housing in many ways frame the larger issue that Massachusetts employers face in attracting and retaining the qualified workers needed to make the economy grow. The commonwealth will succeed only if employees have affordable places to live and an efficient way to get to work and home again.

Transportation touches every corner of our lives. It determines the ability of our fellow citizens to share in the economic prosperity of the commonwealth. It affects housing patterns in a state where housing is in desperately short supply. And it provides the infrastructure for our personal lives, whether it’s visiting the Basketball Hall of Fame in Springfield, catching a Symphony concert or getting to class first thing in the morning.

AIM and its 3,400 member companies care deeply about transportation in all its manifestations. We care about good roads to bring products into and out of manufacturing plants. We care about improving Boston’s dubious status as having the fourth longest traffic delays in the United States. We care about residents of rural areas who find themselves isolated from the economic life of the commonwealth.

That’s why AIM continues to be deeply involved in the effort to create the world-class transportation systems needed by growing Massachusetts employers.

I was privileged to serve last year on Governor Maura’s Healey’s Transportation Funding Task Force, which set the stage for the governor’s new plan to make investments in the state’s roads, bridges and regional transportation system and stabilize the finances of the MBTA. The $8 billion, 10-year initiative would be done without raising taxes and represents the largest state transportation investment in more than 20 years.

AIM is also a member of the Cape & Islands Bridges Coalition and recently hosted a meeting of that group at our offices in Boston. We belong to the group because the replacement of the aging Bourne and Sagamore Bridges represents a desperately needed infrastructure lifeline to an economy that generates $16.3 billion annually – including $1.4 billion from the dynamic tourism industry.

The MBTA remains a centerpiece of state transportation planning, responsible for carrying more than 800,000 riders every weekday on a complex network of subway, light rail, bus, commuter rail and ferry service. The T, which serves approximately 200 communities, is the fourth busiest rapid-transit system in the United States, the third-busiest light rail system.

General Manager Phillip Eng, who has made remarkable progress improving the safety, reliability and performance of the organization, told an AIM Commonwealth Conversation last week that the T is a catalyst for movement and development well beyond the Boston city limits. The agency, for example, is coordinating with Regional Transit Authorities in eastern Massachusetts to ensure end-to-end transportation options for the employees upon which businesses depend.

“We’re moving people and affecting people’s lives and doing it in a positive way,” said Eng, who added that the T has only “scratched the surface” of what is possible.

A final piece of the transportation puzzle is Massport, which manages airports, the seaport, and other infrastructure for international trade in Massachusetts. AIM will host a conversation with Massport CEO Rich Davey on April 8 to update employers on what is happening with the trade gateway to New England. We invite you to join us.

Transportation, like housing, is a sprawling issue with complex financial, governmental and social implications. We must, however, address these implications to prevent our economy from falling victim to its own success.

Updated Oct. 25, 2021, 7:48 a.m. ET

[The South Coast Rail](https://www.mbta.com/projects/south-coast-rail) project promises to bring passenger train service back to Fall River for the first time in more than 60 years. The path to this point has been fraught with detours, false starts, ever-increasing price tags, and broken promises.

The rail project, which started as a proposal in 1991, has passed through the hands of six governors and seen its cost rise by a factor of 25, from $136 million to $3.4 billion.

Let's take a look at how Fall River and the Southcoast had access to passenger rail, lost it, and [is fighting to get it back.](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/business/transportation/2021/03/02/commuter-rail-construction-work-fall-river-kicking-into-gear-south-coast-depot-bridges-layover/6865840002/)

[![Image 1](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/presto/2021/10/22/NHER/352f8a79-df93-4e08-b62c-2978618959ca-Photo_Oct_14_5_31_59_PM.jpg?crop=5183,2916,x0,y263&width=660&height=372&format=pjpg&auto=webp)](https://www.heraldnews.com/picture-gallery/business/transportation/2021/10/25/fall-river-tour-south-coast-rail-station-construction-freetown-fiola-mbta/6129964001/)

Fall River's place in transportation history 
---------------------------------------------

**1844-1854:** Col. Richard Borden builds the city's first railroad in 1844, the Fall River Branch Railroad, linking Fall River with Myricks Junction in Berkley. By 1846, it and two other railroad companies have merged to form the Fall River Railroad, with connections up to Boston. In 1847, the Fall River Railroad starts offering steamship service to New York City, a service that was known as the Fall River Line. The company merged again, this time with Old Colony Railroad, to form Old Colony and Fall River Railroad in 1854.

![Image 2: A postcard of Fall River Station from the early 20th century.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/presto/2021/10/24/NHER/836848db-164e-402c-8916-f733cd728570-fall_river_station.jpg?width=660&height=420&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

**1854-1958:** Old Colony has an extensive network of rail lines across the region, connecting Fall River by train with places like Providence, New Bedford, the Cape, and Boston. The entire Old Colony system falls under the control of the New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad Co. in 1893, giving it a monopoly over transportation in the entire region. In the first half of the 20th century, the rail line undergoes a period of decline due to economic turmoil and competition from the increasingly affordable automobile. The Fall River Line steamship service, once the most famous and luxurious method of travel on the East Coast, is liquidated in 1937. Amid bankruptcy during the Great Depression, Old Colony tries in 1938 to abandon unprofitable lines and 93 stations, including Fall River’s Ferry Street station, but this is reversed in a decision that reaches the Supreme Court in 1939. But the Old Colony rail service in Fall River, along with Taunton and New Bedford will only last less than another 20 years – in 1958, rail service to these cities ends.

**1950s-1960s:** As commercial passenger rail fell into decline, [the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://www.mbta.com/) begins subsidizing railroad companies and then buying commuter rail lines. Over the years, the MBTA returns service to areas that had seen service end. Meanwhile, expressways are built and expanded to connect the Southcoast north -- Route 24 carries Fall River traffic north, while Route 140 connects New Bedford to Taunton and Route 24.

![Image 3: A view of the Fall River Line terminal in New York City from 1937.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/presto/2021/10/24/NHER/dcb9c19d-3e1a-4f1c-96e0-147055431367-Fall_River_line_pier.jpg?width=660&height=537&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Weld's promise kicks off the South Coast Rail push
--------------------------------------------------

**March 1991:** Gov. William Weld asks the state Legislature authorize the sale of MBTA bonds to pay for preliminary engineering and environmental studies to extend commuter rail from Stoughton to southeastern Massachusetts, including Fall River. He’s so confident it will happen under his watch that in February 1992 he proclaims, “Sue me if it doesn’t happen.”

**June 1995:** Anne Galbraith, an MBTA project manager, tells people at a Fall River public hearing that commuters could be boarding trains for Boston by the end of 1997 under a best-case scenario. In a press conference the next month in New Bedford, he promises rail from Fall River and New Bedford to Boston by the fall of 1997.

![Image 4: Former Massachusetts Gov. William Weld poses for a portrait in 2020. Weld served as the governor of Massachusetts from 1991 to 1997.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/presto/2020/01/08/PDEM/5a4b64e8-b53a-466b-8cb3-bf4611c788ac-RS_Weld_010620_.jpg?width=660&height=440&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

**August 1996:** Weld signs a transportation bond bill that includes $136 million to extend commuter rail.

**March-April 1997:** The MBTA releases a study saying the cost to bring commuter rail to Fall River will be closer to $430 million, more than three times the initial estimates. Then-state Rep. Robert Correia says in an interview, “I honestly see it happening. It’s just a question of time.” He suggests the project would likely be up and running by spring of 1999.

**July 1997:** Weld resigns as governor to focus on what becomes an unsuccessful attempt to become ambassador to Mexico. Paul Cellucci becomes governor, and says he is committed to extending rail to Fall River and New Bedford.

![Image 5: In this undated file photo, a commuter train leaves the Middleboro/Lakeville Station on the Old Colony Rail line.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/presto/2021/02/03/NENT/e87ee26b-41ed-4f04-a005-b2b2cca9574d-Middleboro-Lakeville_station_Commuter_Rail_train.jpg?width=660&height=439&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Running out of money, and running into a swamp
----------------------------------------------

**September 1997:** The MBTA’s Old Colony commuter rail line opens, extending service to Middleboro/Lakeville.

**March-April 1998:** The Executive Office of Transportation and Construction authorizes $20 million for the commuter rail design phase. Soon afterward, the House Transportation Committee approves a bill instructing the MBTA to begin construction on a commuter rail extension to Fall River.

**October 1998:** A groundbreaking ceremony is held at the railroad bridge on Turner Street in Fall River for the proposed commuter rail system.

**November 1999:** State Secretary of Environmental Affairs Robert Durand blasts the plan to extend commuter rail to Fall River from Stoughton, saying it would cut through Hockomock Swamp, harm at least six rare species and affect one of the largest and most significant freshwater wetlands in the commonwealth. He’s supported by residents of Raynham and Easton, who fight the extension.

![Image 6: A view of the Hockomock Swamp.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/-mm-/15c99ac303d681770c92d74529048fe3a8184b72/c=0-30-600-368/local/-/media/2020/10/31/Quincy/ghows_gallery-WL-103109999-8ff19cd1.jpg?width=600&height=338&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

**January 2000:** With Gov. Paul Cellucci restating his commitment to extending commuter rail to Fall River, state officials release a new timeline indicating construction will begin by fall 2002 and be completed by 2004.

**July 2002:** The MBTA pushes project start date back to 2007 because it has no money to fund the construction. By now, estimates of the project’s cost have risen from just over $400 million to more than $600 million.

**May 2003:** The MBTA asks the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to halt the environmental permitting process while Gov. Mitt Romney analyzes the cost of the rail extension.

**March-June 2004:** The MBTA does not include funding for an extension to Fall River in its 2004-2009 capital investment plan. Fall River officials meet with Romney, but the governor refuses to commit to bringing rail to Fall River. He eventually agrees to support the rail project in exchange for Fall River lawmakers supporting a project to expand the Sagamore rotary on Cape Cod.

**August 2004:** Romney authorizes more than $430 million for the rail project, though $425 million of that will be released only if the federal government matches it.

**March-April 2005:** Romney releases a long-term transportation plan that includes $670 million for rail to Fall River and New Bedford, and estimates building the extension will take six to eight years. He declares the rail extension is “going to get done” but cautions that it will take more work.

Price tag soars as MBTA focuses on going electric 
--------------------------------------------------

**June 2005:** Douglas Foy, chief of commonwealth development, testifies before the joint committee on Bonding, Capital Expenditures and State Assets that the project’s estimated price tag could now be as high as $1 billion.

![Image 7: Then-Mayor Will Flanagan, center, and Gov. Deval Patrick view track repair work on the Fall River section of the Mass Coastal Railroad in 2014.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/presto/2021/10/24/NHER/7a15e8b1-84b5-4187-94cf-cbcb324810c9-deval_patrick.jpg?width=660&height=493&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

**April 2007:** Gov. Deval Patrick releases “South Coast Rail: A Plan for Action,” detailing the steps that will be taken to bring commuter rail to Fall River and New Bedford. Patrick says the project’s estimated price tag is now $1.4 billion, and that trains will be rolling by December 2016.

**August 2009:** Patrick unveils his $1.4 billion plan to build a long-promised commuter rail project linking New Bedford and Fall River to Boston, saying it would create up to 3,800 permanent jobs by the year 2030 and generate nearly $500 million in economic activity.

**September 2009:** State finalizes a deal with CSX to purchase rail lines in New Bedford and Fall River.

**January 2013:** Patrick unveils another new state transportation plan that calls for spending $10 billion over 10 years, including the South Coast Rail line between Fall River and Boston by 2021 -- by now, with a $1.8 billion estimated price tag.

![Image 8: The MBTA train depot in Stoughton.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/-mm-/b46158a8388b70656aad27c7567a0c37ef8e405c/c=0-126-2500-1532/local/-/media/2020/11/02/WickedLocal/ghows-WL-201007962-2030c47e.jpg?width=660&height=372&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

**June 2013:** The Army Corps of Engineers determines a route to the Southcoast from Stoughton using electric trains will have the least environmental impact. A state report identifies this route as the preferred route for South Coast Rail.

**June 2014:** MassDOT awards a 10-year contract for up to $210 million for South Coast Rail. Patrick hails this as “a game changer” to move the project from the planning to construction stage. By now, the price tag has risen to an estimated $2.3 billion.

**November 2014-January 2016:** The South Coast Rail project pushes slowly forward as seven railroad freight bridges are replaced.

![Image 9: Phase 1 of the South Coast Rail plan will continue service from Middleboro, splitting in Berkley to separate lines going to Fall River and New Bedford.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/presto/2021/10/24/NHER/d16137ba-7ef2-4481-99aa-c00207c082b5-map.jpg?width=660&height=325&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Back to the drawing board, and South Coast Rail gets a two-part plan
--------------------------------------------------------------------

**June 2016:** MassDOT and the MBTA say that by now, the cost of South Coast Rail using electric trains from Stoughton has risen to $3.4 billion, and the construction schedule would need to be delayed another seven years. Given that development, they revisit a previously rejected plan – to extend the rail line from Middleboro/Lakeville using diesel trains, saying that it would cost a lot less and be constructed sooner.

**March 2017:** Gov. Charlie Baker’s administration agrees on a new course for South Coast Rail. Phase 1 would continue diesel train service from Middleboro/Lakeville, splitting at Myricks Junction for separate lines to Fall River and New Bedford, at a cost of just over $1 billion. The project is slated to start in 2019 and be complete by 2024. Meanwhile, engineering, design and permitting work will continue on the “full build” of the South Coast Rail project – electric rail service from Stoughton, estimated to cost over $3 billion and be complete by 2030.

![Image 10: After years of waiting, Gov. Charlie Baker, along with many other state and local politicians, break ground on South Coast Rail off of Chace Road in Freetown in 2019.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/presto/2021/10/24/NHER/4083c9e3-00d9-4587-83e7-7d9f3a79f89e-groundbreaking.jpg?width=660&height=454&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

**June 2019:** Baker and political leaders from across the region meet in Freetown for a groundbreaking ceremony.

**2019-2021:** Construction continues on the South Coast Rail project, which includes making rail improvements, rebuilding rail bridges, building two new layover facilities in Fall River and New Bedford, and building and six new stations. MBTA officials say the project remains on schedule and on budget, and is expected to be running by the end of 2023.

_Dan Medeiros can be reached at [dmedeiros@heraldnews.com](mailto:dmedeiros@heraldnews.com). Support local journalism by purchasing a digital or print subscription to The Herald News today._

The [MBTA](http://boston.com/tag/mbta) is extending free weekend service after a tumultuous first month for the new South Coast Rail extension, which now connects some commuters to Boston for the first time in 65 years.

The new line to Fall River, New Bedford, and Taunton has been plagued by shuttle buses, canceled trips, and frequent delays since its first trains began March 24, according to the MBTA and Keolis Commuter Services, which operates the commuter rail.

The MBTA announced last week that shuttle buses will replace service on April 19 and 20, and, “as a show of gratitude to the riders who have been utilizing this new service,” fare-free weekend service would be [extended through May](https://www.mbta.com/news/2025-04-18/service-changes-planned-fall-rivernew-bedford-line-weekend).

Advertisement:

Some weekend service on the Fall River/New Bedford line has even been canceled due to staffing issues, a Keolis spokesperson confirmed. While weekday service hasn’t been affected, the MBTA’s Commuter Rail Alerts reported daily issues with the line, including delays, shuttle buses, and cancellations, in part due to staffing issues.

_The Boston Globe_ reported that about 75 riders were [stranded at East Taunton](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2025/04/23/metro/south-coast-rail-service-disruptions/) when a shuttle bus to Fall River didn’t show up on April 13, a Sunday.

“While the last two weekends did not perform the levels that our riders deserve, we remain committed to this schedule,” MBTA General Manager Phillip Eng said in a statement. “Keolis has assured us that in addition to the hiring and training done to date, they are focused on continuing accelerated qualification of staff until each and every employee is fully qualified to operate on all territory including the new South Coast Rail.”

**Keolis plans to higher more qualified conductors**
----------------------------------------------------

The line’s cancellations are sometimes due to crew member illness, and Keolis said it is working to increase the number of qualified conductors to fill in shifts.

Advertisement:

To ensure reliability, Keolis and the MBTA are planning to employ 65 qualified conductors to operate the South Coast Rail by early June. Currently, there are 54 qualified conductors, the Keolis spokesperson said.

##### South Coast Rail

*   [![Image 4](https://bdc2020.o0bc.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/s3___bgmp-arc_arc-feeds_generic-photos_to-arc_ryanSouthCoastRail3met-67e30527f375f-768x432.jpg) #### South Coast Rail schedule has some readers ‘deeply disappointed’](https://www.boston.com/community/readers-say/2025/03/25/south-coast-rail-schedule-has-some-readers-deeply-disappointed/?p1=article_recirc_inline_feature)
*   [#### 3 things to know about the new rail line connecting southeastern Mass. to Boston](https://www.boston.com/news/transportation/2025/03/24/3-things-to-know-about-the-new-rail-line-connecting-southeastern-mass-to-boston/?p1=article_recirc_inline_feed)

“Keolis apologizes to the passengers and communities served by the Fall River/New Bedford Line,” the Boston-based company said. “Keolis understands your frustration, and we are working to improve reliability and resilience going forward.”

The MBTA noted that Keolis will be fined more than $51,000 for the cancellations and terminations due to crew issues. Before the South Coast Rail launched, Eng said that Keolis “confirmed their readiness.”

“Like our riders, we are not pleased with the need to replace selected trains with buses on weekends, and we apologize for these disruptions,” Eng said in a statement, while noting that weekday service has been more consistent than weekends. “Robust all-day service is important to those who use mass transit and we are confident that we can, and will, turn this around.”

[TransitMatters](https://transitmatters.org/), a Boston transit advocacy group, blamed South Coast Rail’s “ambitious timeline” for the shortage of qualified staff. The line has been in development for decades, with years of delays, and cost billions of dollars.

Advertisement:

“The ambitious timeline for the South Coast Rail rollout led to this gap in capacity despite the relatively sparse planned service,” Program Assistant Janet Cheung wrote in an email. “We hope to see better coordination in the future with staffing and service changes.”

MBTA explains South Coast Rail train delays, cancellations. Senator demands accountability
==========================================================================================

 [![Image 1: Portrait of Frank Mulligan](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/gcdn/presto/2021/06/11/NWKL/c4f67958-f757-4fe5-ab68-59c73d9cea17-IMG_9461.JPG?crop=1996,1996,x0,y257&width=48&height=48&format=pjpg&auto=webp) Frank Mulligan](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/staff/5955970002/frank-mulligan/)

Keep Watching

*   State Sen. Mark Montigny has asked the MBTA to explain delays and cancellations of trains on the Fall River/New Bedford Line.
*   The MBTA has responded with information and data about how many conductors need to be hired and what happens in event of cancellations.

BOSTON — It’s estimated that [cancellations of South Coast Rail trains](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/04/29/mbta-has-until-friday-to-respond-on-south-coast-rail-cancellations/83341354007/) on the Fall River/New Bedford Line left a total of 15 people stranded between its March 24 debut and May 2.

That estimate came from the MBTA and commuter rail line operator Keolis.

“Following a review of available customer service data, we estimate fewer than 15 people,” they said in a response to [questions from state Sen. Mark Montigny](https://subscribe.heraldnews.com/restricted?return=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.heraldnews.com%2Fstory%2Fnews%2F2025%2F04%2F29%2Fmbta-has-until-friday-to-respond-on-south-coast-rail-cancellations%2F83341354007%2F&gps-source=CPROADBLOCKDH&itm_source=roadblock&itm_medium=onsite&itm_campaign=2025BAUREFRESHJZ&gca-cat=p&gca-uir=true&gca-epti=z11xx83e004400v11xx83b00xxxxd11xx65&gca-ft=9&gca-ds=sophi&sltsgmt=0150_A&offer=W-JZ), D-New Bedford.

His Senate Committee on Post Audit and Oversight is investigating the delays and cancellations that have marred the long-awaited [rail line’s first six weeks](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/03/28/mbta-commuter-rail-to-new-bedford-schedule-apps-cost-and-more-info/82697378007/).

In requesting the information from MBTA General Manager Phil Eng, Montigny wrote, “The sudden cancellation of train service stranded passengers, many of them families with children, more than 50 miles from home.”

South Coast Rail on weekends: [What's the schedule? What apps do you need? What to know](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/03/28/mbta-commuter-rail-to-new-bedford-schedule-apps-cost-and-more-info/82697378007/)

![Image 2: Passengers take photos as they prepare to board the train from New Bedford to Boston on opening day of the Fall River/New Bedford commuter rail line. It’s estimated that 15 people have been left stranded on the line between its March 24 debut and May 2.](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/05/06/sen-montigny-demands-answers-on-poor-rail-performance-from-mbta/83463056007/)

MBTA, Keolis apologize to passengers with negative experiences
--------------------------------------------------------------

He gave Eng a May 2 deadline to respond to 15 questions, which has been met. Montigny released the answers on May 5.

The MBTA-Keolis response included, “It is never acceptable to leave any number of passengers without access to train service. The MBTA and our commuter rail operator, Keolis, apologize to every passenger who had a negative experience. Keolis is actively undertaking efforts to qualify all south side conductors and engineers, as well as managers, to ensure weekend train crew coverage for the Fall River and New Bedford lines as soon as possible. In addition, Keolis is providing local and express bus service to replace all Fall River/New Bedford weekend trains not operated due to crew availability until the crew coverage issue is resolved.”

![Image 3: Senator Mark Montigny is framed by the photo of a train in the background during the grand opening ceremony of the Fall River/New Bedford commuter rail line serving the SouthCoast held in the new East Taunton train station.](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/05/06/sen-montigny-demands-answers-on-poor-rail-performance-from-mbta/83463056007/)

How many South Coast Rail trains have been delayed or canceled, and why?
------------------------------------------------------------------------

*   Thirty trains were cancelled from March 28 to April 25. Of those 30, nine were due to insufficient staffing, five were due to mechanical failure, two were due to trespassers on tracks, one was due to slippery rail, one was due to the engine.
*   Of the nine trips that couldn’t be completed from March 28 to April 22, one was due to insufficient staffing, one was due to a trespasser on the tracks, and seven were caused by problems with the engine.
*   232 trains were at least 10 minutes late from March 24 through April 27. Of those, the two longest delays were 134 and 139 minutes, and both were for trespassers on the tracks. Eight were late due to insufficient staffing. Most of the late trains were under 20 minutes late.

Montigny says 'Keolis must be held accountable'
-----------------------------------------------

Montigny said he has been frustrated by the lack of proper staffing and management that has led to the significant delays and cancellations.

“While this situation is completely unacceptable and downright frustrating, I appreciate the general manager’s timely and thorough response to our inquiry and his commitment to resolving this issue,” Montigny said.

He added, “Keolis must be held accountable to deliver timely and consistent service and it appears that the MBTA shares this perspective.”

![Image 4: Passengers wait for the New Bedford to Boston train to arrive on opening day of the Fall River/New Bedford commuter rail line serving the SouthCoast from East Taunton.](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/05/06/sen-montigny-demands-answers-on-poor-rail-performance-from-mbta/83463056007/)

In response to frequent delays and cancellations, the MBTA extended its free weekend service to and from South Coast Rail stations until June 1. It was initially set to expire at the end of April.

Montigny said free weekends through June 1 isn’t enough for riders when they have to take a bus home. “The T should make every effort to offer an extended free service when the staffing issues are resolved later this spring,” he stated.

He said his committee will keep the investigation open in the meantime, “pending satisfactory staffing levels and adherence to the service schedule.”

Back in business: [State and local officials celebrate commuter rail’s return to New Bedford 70 years later](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/03/24/south-coast-rail-starts-new-bedford-to-boston/82640096007/)

Keolis says more train conductors coming on board
-------------------------------------------------

Keolis has said of crew availability: "Crew members, including conductors and engineers, must be qualified in order to operate trains on specific lines. If a crew member calls out sick or misses their shift, it can cause trains to be cancelled if a qualified person cannot be found to replace them."

Keolis also said that the company was working to increase the number of conductors for South Coast Rail, with a plan to have 65 "qualified conductors" by early June.

The Fall River/New Bedford Line opened with 41 qualified conductors, according to the information provided to Montigny, which had been Keolis’ goal. The company is subject to fines for providing insufficient staff, the MBTA noted.

What happens when passengers are stranded? Keolis has 'rapid response' plan
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Keolis’ plan in case of strandings is “designed for a rapid response,” according to the information provided to Montigny.

“Once a train cancellation is confirmed, Keolis dispatchers immediately notify its bus vendors if a rescue train isn't available. In general, the goal is to have shuttle buses en route to affected stations within about 30 minutes of confirmation, and to begin carrying passengers within roughly an hour of the cancellation. This timeline can vary with factors like time of day or location, but the emphasis is on speedy relief. To further ensure customer safety, Uber or taxi may be utilized when needed at no expense to the passenger if bus options are not available.”

MA officials warn of $1.2B cost overrun, 8-year delay for South Coast rail project
==================================================================================

 Published June 29, 2016 

By

### **Dive Brief:**

*   The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority has announced that its South Coast rail project, originally scheduled for completion in 2022 at a cost of $2.23 billion, will now cost $3.4 billion and won’t be finished until 2030, the Boston Herald reported.
*   MBTA officials said that the permitting process alone could take more than six years, largely due to environmental issues raised by the agency’s first electric train system, which involves work to 75 miles of existing track, upgrades to 36 bridges and the purchase of new locomotives and cars.
*   The prospect of increased costs and significant delays has prompted the MBTA to look at alternatives to the South Coast Rail, including the addition of a second track to an existing underground line and expansion of existing service.

### **Dive Insight**

Transportation Secretary Stephanie Pollack told reporters that the governor and MBTA “are 100% committed to getting trains to the South Coast” but that she is concerned with how long it will take to deliver the long-promised service, as well as the rising costs, according to the Herald. MBTA officials said that $4.1 million will be added to the total project cost for each month it is delayed.

The MBTA is also still struggling to get a handle on its Green Line rail extension, which was derailed after [cost overruns](https://www.constructiondive.com/news/cost-of-grossly-overpriced-boston-green-line-extension-could-reach-642m/411505/) and delays [led to the firing](https://www.constructiondive.com/news/white-skanska-kiewit-ousted-from-over-budget-boston-green-line-extension-pr/410649/) of the project’s lead contractor, the joint venture of White-Skanska-Kiewit (WSK). MBTA officials [initially blamed the rail’s problems](https://www.constructiondive.com/news/critics-blame-soaring-costs-of-boston-rail-line-on-white-skanska-kiewit-max/405629/) on the guaranteed maximum price delivery method, but since WSK’s termination, reports from outside consultants have emerged [pointing to mismanagement](https://www.constructiondive.com/news/report-depicts-bleak-picture-of-boston-rail-line-extension-project-1b-ov/410081/) by MBTA officials and consultants.

Most recently, the MBTA [voted to move forward](https://www.constructiondive.com/news/update-scaled-down-23b-boston-green-line-extension-scores-support-from/418923/) with what it referred to as a [“scaled down” version](https://www.constructiondive.com/news/mbta-presents-1st-round-of-drastic-cuts-to-boston-green-line-extension/415023/) of the Green Line—a $2.3 billion variant that will see a deletion of some convenience elements, like escalators and elevators, as well as more austere stations. The rail is also getting a new delivery method,[design-build](https://www.constructiondive.com/news/the-dotted-line-how-design-build-can-create-a-symphony-of-collaboration/415589/),and the MBTA said it will train its staff on the method to avoid a repeat cost and scheduling boondoggle.

South Coast Rail isn’t a project anymore. Trains brimmed with excitement and optimism on Monday’s rides to Boston, the first in 67 years. ![Image 3: Avatar photo](https://newbedfordlight.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/cropped-cropped-456-edited-80x80.jpg) by [Grace Ferguson](https://newbedfordlight.org/author/gfergusonnewbedfordlight-org/) March 24, 2025March 25, 2025 ### Share this: * [Click to email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email](mailto:?subject=%5BShared%20Post%5D%20Rail%20returns%20to%20New%20Bedford%C2%A0&body=https%3A%2F%2Fnewbedfordlight.org%2Frail-returns-to-new-bedford%2F&share=email) * [Click to share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook](https://newbedfordlight.org/rail-returns-to-new-bedford/?share=facebook) * [Click to share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky](https://newbedfordlight.org/rail-returns-to-new-bedford/?share=bluesky) * [Click to share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn](https://newbedfordlight.org/rail-returns-to-new-bedford/?share=linkedin) * [Click to share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp](https://newbedfordlight.org/rail-returns-to-new-bedford/?share=jetpack-whatsapp) * [Click to print (Opens in new window) Print](https://newbedfordlight.org/rail-returns-to-new-bedford/#print?share=print) ![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/newbedfordlight.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Image_20250324_042959_918-scaled-1.jpeg?fit=1200%2C815&ssl=1) Passengers smile for a selfie aboard the first South Coast Rail train to depart New Bedford for South Station on Monday. Credit: Anastasia E. Lennon / The New Bedford Light
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
Believe it. Dozens of people saw the first MBTA commuter rail train pull into New Bedford Station just before 4:27 a.m. on Monday. They heard the conductor shout “all aboard!” South Coast Rail isn’t a project anymore — it’s a real commuter rail line you can ride. “I thought this day would never come,” said Rick Platt, a conductor on the 7:25 a.m. train leaving New Bedford Station. It only started to feel real to him when crews began training a few weeks ago. ![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/newbedfordlight.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Image_20250324_043616_360-edited-1024x576.jpeg?resize=780%2C439&ssl=1) The first South Coast Rail train this morning in New Bedford. Credit: Grace Ferguson / The New Bedford Light Trains brimmed with excitement and optimism. Passengers cheered when they felt their train lurch forward toward Boston. Railroad staff passed out pins, magnets, and commemorative spikes like candy. Just to sweeten the celebrations, the MBTA [made fares free](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-mbta-announce-free-south-coast-rail-service-through-the-end-of-march) this week and every weekend through the end of April. The frustration that the South Coast had built up over decades of delays seemed to fade away. In one train car, people even broke into [song](https://newbedfordlight.org/first-train-departs-on-time/#:~:text=Singing%20the%20South%20Coast%20Rail%20song). Train enthusiast Evan Bouwens passed around sheets with original lyrics to the tune of “She’ll Be Coming ’Round the Mountain” on the first train out of New Bedford. _“March 24th of 2025,_ _The South Coast Rail has finally arrived!_ _Years in the making, now deliver_ _To New Bedford and Fall River!_ _What a day! We’re glad to be alive!”_ ![Image 6: YouTube video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/Uea6aifBaoQ/hqdefault.jpg) At a [jubilant ribbon-cutting](https://newbedfordlight.org/gov-healey-mayor-vips-celebrate-opening-of-south-coast-rail/) in Taunton, dozens of officials celebrated this day as a triumph. If not for the South Coast’s relentless advocacy, they said, the extension could not have been built. “Today is more than just your typical ribbon-cutting ceremony,” Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll said to a packed house. “This is a historic milestone for the South Coast.” For the first time [in 67 years](https://newbedfordlight.org/key-points-on-the-route-to-south-coast-rail-2/#:~:text=Sept.%205%2C%201958%3A%20The%20last%20train%20to%20Boston%20leaves%20New%20Bedford), New Bedford has a passenger rail connection to Boston. This project has faced constant stops and starts since it was first promised in the early 1990s. As recently as last spring, it had no official schedule for completion. [A recent timeline](https://newbedfordlight.org/south-coast-rail-2025-mbta-phil-eng-karen-antion/) had included a May 2025 launch date, but the MBTA beat its own goal by two months. Virginia Callas, a 98-year-old New Bedford resident, [remembered](https://newbedfordlight.org/98-year-old-sees-excited-for-south-coast-rail-in-new-bedford/) the trains that served the city before the New Haven Railroad stopped running them in 1958. She crossed an item off her bucket list when she rode the MBTA train from New Bedford to East Taunton on Monday. “I’m just so lucky to be sitting in this train,” she said after finding her seat. “If it doesn’t go anywhere, I’m happy.” The first three early-morning trains left New Bedford Station right on time, as if they were cruising straight out of New Bedford’s dreams. But [delays set in after sunrise](https://newbedfordlight.org/delays-affect-south-coast-rail-on-first-day/). Most midday trains ran slightly late, some as much as 20 to 30 minutes behind. Times mostly recovered by the evening commute, though. ![Image 7](https://i0.wp.com/newbedfordlight.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/1839.jpg?resize=780%2C519&ssl=1) Passengers sit on the first ride from Boston to Fall River reading the news and the new train schedule. Credit: Eleonora Bianchi / The New Bedford Light A spokesperson for Keolis, the company that operates the commuter rail network, did not directly address The Light’s questions about the delays. In Boston, some passengers looking for the Middleborough/Lakeville line were confused — that’s because it was renamed to the Fall River/New Bedford line overnight, and the schedule was overhauled to accommodate the new service. Keolis employees said about 30% of commuters had questions about the 6:45 a.m. train from Boston to Fall River and New Bedford. * * * ### [Local news needs your support before the year ends ⇢](https://newbedfordlight.org/support-our-publication/) * * * Overall, the disruptions were minor. And they had no impact on the joyful vibe aboard the train New Bedford’s VIPs took to the ribbon-cutting in Taunton. “I’m elated, I’m excited, and I’m reinvigorated,” said New Bedford City Councilor Ian Abreu. ![Image 8](https://i0.wp.com/newbedfordlight.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/South-Station-Rail-032425.jpg?resize=512%2C384&ssl=1) Commuters wait in Boston’s South Station Monday for the New Bedford/Fall River line’s first outbound run to be assigned a platform. Tony Sapienza, who chairs the boards of the New Bedford Economic Development Council and the Whaling Museum, called the experience a “dream come true.” Former New Bedford Mayor John Bullard said it felt “fantastic” to be on the train. Both said they were looking forward to the prospect of new development spurred by the extension. Many residents have feared that South Coast Rail would increase housing costs and displace residents. Paul Chasse, CEO of the REALTOR Association of Southeastern Massachusetts and leader of the Rail to Boston Coalition, isn’t among them. “I don’t think it’s going to gentrify the city,” he said before hopping on the train. “It will have more pros than cons.” The pros include more job opportunities for locals and more money spent by visitors to South Coast businesses, he said. The bottom line for Chasse and virtually every other person who spoke publicly on Monday: South Coast Rail will be good for New Bedford’s economy. ![Image 9](https://i0.wp.com/newbedfordlight.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/mayorSCR032425.jpg?resize=780%2C585&ssl=1) New Bedford Mayor Jon Mitchell speaks at Monday’s ribbon-cutting for South Coast Rail, saying the project is about persistence. ### **Fulfilling a promise** Deborah Baker and her husband William Baker made a promise to each other: When South Coast Rail finally launched, they would ride the train together to Boston. * * * Get local news delivered straight to your inbox. ------------------------------------------------ * Daily Newsletter A dose of New Bedford news in your inbox each weekday morning * The Weekender Catch up on the week’s biggest stories every Saturday morning Sign up * * * That was years ago, as the two New England natives — she from Wellesley, he from Belmont — vacationed near New Bedford and heard about the prospect of a rail link into Boston. “We always said it would be great to live in a place where you could get to Boston” without driving, she said. They moved around the East Coast, down to Florida in the late 1990s, then back to New England in 2009, to New Bedford, where they lived in a house just south of downtown in Ward 5. And, like so many others, waited for the train. And waited. The day came on Monday. Too late for William Baker, who died in November 2022. The founder and executive director of The Dyslexia Foundation, which conducted research and advocacy on the condition, was 71 years old. “I am fulfilling a promise I made to my husband,” said Deborah, who boarded the 2:13 p.m. train from the downtown station. As the train rolled on toward Middleborough, she said her husband was indeed with her, as she reached into her handbag. She pulled out a tin of cinnamon Altoids, emptied of the mints. She said that some of her husband’s remains had been scattered two years ago at Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris, where visitors can find the graves of such cultural luminaries as Oscar Wilde, Marcel Proust and Richard Wright, Frederic Chopin, Sarah Bernhardt and Jim Morrison. And some of William Baker’s ashes were in the Altoids tin, along for the ride to Boston. Deborah Baker figured she’d get a coffee at South Station, then get a train back, wrapping up a tribute to promises fulfilled and perseverance. She said she and her husband would often say to each other: “The train is coming back. We just 100 percent believed it was coming back.” _New Bedford Light reporters Eleonora Bianchi, Arthur Hirsch, Colin Hogan, Anastasia Lennon, Abigail Pritchard, and Jack Spillane contributed to this Jan. 7, 2025Updated Jan. 8, 2025, 12:22 p.m. ET

_This story was updated because an earlier version included an inaccuracy and to add new information._

Close to 70 years after the last train departed, southeastern Massachusetts is [preparing to reconnect with Boston](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2024/12/30/south-coast-rail-and-more-fall-rivers-2025-in-transportation/77267793007/).

South Coast Rail, [expected to launch public service in spring 2025](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2024/10/18/mbta-puts-south-coast-rail-highway-signs-in-fall-river-60-second-read/75721047007/), promises to transform the job market, economic conditions and regional connectivity by restoring direct service to Fall River, New Bedford and Taunton, the only major cities within a 50-mile radius of the state capital that lack commuter rail access to the city, according to the Massachusetts Department of Transportation.

But for communities already grappling with [housing affordability crises](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2024/10/16/housing-group-fall-river-needs-affordable-rent-to-fight-homelessness/75675071007/), the long-awaited rail link raises questions about who will benefit.

Housing advocates warn that the project could exacerbate a crisis for [low-income families](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/local/2024/12/13/need-an-affordable-apartment-in-fall-river-guidelines-and-locations/76827210007/) and push longtime residents out of their neighborhoods.

“Without thoughtful planning, the rail will benefit some people, but might also deepen existing inequities and perpetuate the current affordable housing crisis for lower-income residents,” said Judith Liben, a housing attorney at the Boston-based Massachusetts Law Reform Institute.

![Image 1: MBTA train crossing at 65 Chase Road in East Freetown on Monday June 17, 2024.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2024/06/17/NHER/74131098007-mbta-train-5.jpg?crop=2400,1592,x0,y0&width=660&height=438&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Fall River already facing housing challenges
--------------------------------------------

Liben, who recently authored a report analyzing Fall River’s housing strategies, identified a series of challenges confronting low-income and working-class renters in the city.

Surging rents, high housing cost burdens, increasing evictions and a vacancy rate of just 1.2% have made affordable housing increasingly elusive for many residents, the report finds.

It also reveals that the city has prioritized the development of market-rate and luxury housing units while neglecting affordable housing needs and a comprehensive plan to address them.

“There are increasing evictions and fears of displacement,” said Liben. “And these are not just problems in Fall River, but you've seen them replicated in other places.”

![Image 2: Vehicles travel on Route 18 north bound in New Bedford, under the new pedestrian bridge connecting Purchase Street to the new rail train station, as the old one can be seen in the distance.](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/01/07/south-coast-rail-will-affect-fall-river-new-bedford-housing-markets/77495841007/)

New Bedford has taken a different approach
------------------------------------------

The MLRI report pointed to New Bedford as a model for a more balanced approach to addressing its housing crisis.

With plans to expand both market-rate and mixed-income housing, the report positions New Bedford to pursue more equitable growth compared to neighboring communities.

These strategies are informed by challenges identified in a MassINC study, which examined New Bedford’s residential market and found that over two-thirds of renters would be unable to afford typical asking rents if forced to move.

Another study by MassINC surveying the housing market in gateway cities highlights a decade-long trend of household growth outpacing housing stock growth from 2012 to 2022, tightening markets and reducing vacancy rates.

During that period, Fall River grew by 3,395 households, while on-market units increased by only 1,564, exacerbating the housing shortage. New Bedford saw a smaller but still significant gap, with households growing by 2,563 compared to an increase of 1,744 on-market units.

Over the next year, home values in both cities are expected to climb, driven by a combination of factors that may include the upcoming South Coast Rail and broader market trends.

Home values in Fall River are projected to rise by an average of 1.2% by Feb. 28, 2025, and further increase to 3.5% by Nov. 30, 2025, compared to values at the end of last month, an analysis of Zillow’s home value forecast data shows.

New Bedford is expected to see a similar trend, with home values predicted to grow by 1.1% by Feb. 28, 2025, and 3.35% by Nov. 30, 2025.

Building transit-oriented development near the train
----------------------------------------------------

The introduction of commuter rail is expected to bring opportunities for transit-oriented development, a strategy that typically involves creating mixed-use developments near transit stations to stimulate local economies, attract businesses and encourage residential growth, according to the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority.

A report by MassINC highlights the transformative potential of transit-oriented development in gateway cities. With large swaths of vacant and underutilized land surrounding commuter rail stations, these cities have the opportunity to create thousands of new housing units and jobs.

But Liben argues, “housing for whom?”

The MBTA Communities Act, passed in 2021, mandates municipalities served by MBTA transit, including commuter rail, establish zoning districts permitting multi-family housing to be built as of right.

![Image 4: The Freetown station of the South Coast Rail has been completed.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/presto/2022/12/05/NHER/76b9728a-ede6-4cfa-b8fb-be655b211983-scr1.jpg?width=660&height=396&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

As MBTA communities, both Fall River and New Bedford are required to comply with the law to increase housing supply.

Fall River is compliant with the MBTA Communities Act. New Bedford has interim compliance, with its application under review.

Although the legislation focuses on increasing the overall supply of multi-family housing near transit areas, it does not explicitly require that this housing be designated as affordable or reserved for low-income residents.

Liben emphasized the importance of equitable development as new housing is introduced near the rail stations.

“We anticipate there will be a lot more housing, but it should be housing that is to some extent available to a broad income spectrum and not just wealthy people,” she said.

![Image 5: Neighborhood behind the new T stop at Depot St. in Fall River June 4, 2024.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2024/06/04/NHER/73975049007-t-6.jpg?width=660&height=461&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

For Paulo J. Amaral, a longtime resident of Fall River and former City Council candidate, the commuter rail represents both opportunity and challenge.

From a municipality standpoint, he said, an influx of people will boost the local economy and businesses, but low-income residents will suffer the most.

“You have a lot of people from up north coming to Fall River because they're being displaced or they can't afford to be there,” Amaral said. “They come in here and the same thing is going to happen to Fall River. So it's a pro and con.”

Fall River may have to adapt
----------------------------

As residents brace for the changes brought by the South Coast Rail, Amaral acknowledged that progress is inevitable.

“It's in the eye of the beholder, some people are going to win, some people are going to lose,” he said. “This is what happens in a society – things change, things are dynamic, they're fluid and you got to adapt and adjust.”

Housing advocates like Liben stress the importance of the city setting clear affordable housing goals, adopting strong inclusionary zoning ordinances and maximizing the use of state and federal resources to increase affordable housing and prevent displacement.

“It’s wonderful the train is coming, but the city has to make sure that all of its residents benefit by the train coming and none of the residents are hurt by the train coming,” she said.
